items.title: Traefik from 2.11.58 before 2.11.61 Denial of Service via NTLM/Negotiate Headers
items.summary: Classification: Severe, Solution: Official Fix, Exploit Maturity: Not Defined, CVSSv3.1: 8.7, CVEs: CVE-2026-130732, Summary: Traefik from 2.11.58 before 2.11.61 contains a resource leak vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to exhaust resources by sending Authorization headers with NTLM or Negotiate schemes. Attackers can open many short-lived connections that each allocate a dedicated backend transport never released, exhausting memory, file descriptors and backend connections.

items.title: Major African Stock Exchange Targeted in AI-Assisted Attack
items.summary: Symantec's Threat Hunter Team found a toolkit on a stock exchange in an African country with multiple traits that suggest it was written, or at least assisted, by an AI model. A 41-module PowerShell toolkit with all the hallmarks of AI authorship tested credentials and API keys against the exchange's investment API and a securities depository gateway.

items.title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits vSphere
items.summary: On Nov. 19, 2026, VMware disclosed CVE-2026-123890, which impacts VMware vCenter Server deployments. vSphere consists of both ESXi (the hypervisor) and vCenter Server. ARMORY CASTLE exploited this vulnerability in early September 2026 using BONESAW, according to forensic evidence. BONESAW is a utility primarily built to facilitate remote exploitation written in Golang , which utilizes CVE-2026-123890 to exfiltrate the arbitrary Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), hijack the SAML Security Token Service (STS), and create a Single Sign On (SSO) Administrator account. ARMORY CASTLE’s use of BONESAW represents significant new insight into this threat actor’s post-exploitation tactics. In this campaign, ARMORY CASTLE exploited two zero-days, and deployed three sets of malware specifically tailored for operating on targeted devices, indicating deep platform expertise and substantial resource backing. We are publishing this analysis, along with mitigation and hardening guidance, to support defenders in detecting this threat.

items.title: The Dream of the 1990s Is Alive Again in Cybersecurity
items.summary: If you were involved in either offensive or defensive security in any capacity back in the 90s or 2000s, you probably remember the cadence. Someone found a devastating vulnerability in software that everybody depended on. You dropped what you were doing, figured out where you were exposed, and either raced to fix it (if you were in the early cybersecurity industry of the time) or exploit it (if you were in EFNet IRC channels). Then it happened again the next week. Luckily, we’ve been through this before. Taking the experiences from the first prolific zero-day era and applying it to today, combined with recent conversations with the CISOs of the most AI native security programs, a few themes are emerging about what the next few years will look like.

items.title: Russia’s FIMI and malicious cyber activities: Council imposes sanctions on 30 individuals and two entities
items.summary: Today the Council is also listing NoName057(16), a pro-Russian hacker group that first emerged in March 2022, following the Russian invasion of Ukraine and claims responsibility for cyber-attacks on government bodies, critical infrastructure, and private companies of Ukraine, the United States of America and EU member states. In the EU, NoName057(16) has targeted websites and portals from multiple sectors, using Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks. The energy, financial and transport sectors, water supply facilities, as well as political parties and candidates during electoral processes were notably targeted. Those subjects to these restrictive measures are exposed to an asset freeze and travel bans which prevent them from entering or transiting through EU member states. Furthermore, EU citizens and companies are forbidden from making funds available to them directly or indirectly.

items.title: phpAfterShell: From Interrupted Session Writes to Remote Code Execution
items.summary: TL;DR: PHP can update a file-backed session while parsing an unauthenticated multipart request, even before the target script begins execution. We discovered reliable methods to interrupt the file operation during session upload-progress updates, allowing us to splice the prefix of one valid session with the suffix of another. A subsequent session operation treats the corrupted data as legitimate server-side state, giving attackers control over session values and the ability to trigger object deserialization. By chaining this primitive with a memory-corruption in a PHP-native class, we achieved remote code execution. We reported this vulnerability to the PHP team, and it was assigned CVE-2026-126714, with a critical CVSS score of 9.2. The php2shell patch [...] stopped objects from becoming active during the RFC1867 callback. It did not make the Session file update safe when a worker died. The bytes could remain on disk and become active later, when the application called session_start(). The original exploit stopped working, but the underlying problem was still there.

items.title: Researcher Demonstrates Database RCE Exploits Affecting PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle
items.summary: Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL. The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack. The work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, plan, and execute a query. Four of the flaws now have vendor CVEs and fixes, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack.

items.title: European Commission confirms cyberattack, says hackers used AI tool
items.summary: POLITICO first reported that the Commission had been impacted by the cyberattack. It said CERT-EU had identified the attackers’ use of ARTEX, an open-source AI hacking platform that the FBI last week warned was being used both by criminals and state-sponsored groups. The attack reportedly disrupted the European Commission’s personnel systems for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements and translation services. A commission spokesperson confirmed to Recorded Future News they had “taken the necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign,” including taking several services offline as “a protective measure.” Regnier said investigators had found no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly and were unaware of any ransom demand. He said the investigation remains open. Asked why the incident was not disclosed earlier, Regnier said publicizing defensive measures could undermine their effectiveness. “There was no hiding whatsoever,” he told journalists.

items.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
items.summary: 1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence 2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved 3. Check trusted sources of network data 4. Look for claims of responsibility 5. Sit tight and reserve judgment
